      I will refer to him as Mr. S. He taught Spanish in my high school. Before I get into it, I should mention that I had a "little" "crush" on him, so that may be a source of bias here. Ehhmmm. . . So, honestly, I was totally in love with him (: That's a little odd, to be in love with a teacher, right? Maybe, but I'm not exaggerating. I really did love him, and I still do! First experience with unrequited love. Good stuff. Uh, now to move on to the salient stuff. . .

      Mr. S was probably the most loved teacher in the whole school. Everybody liked him, and for good reason: He was confident, kind, cheerful, vibrant, and funny. He clicked really well with all the students. His natural charisma made it easier to be interested in and inspired by him.

      I was moved by Mr. S's investment in his work. People don't really take high school Spanish seriously, but their disregard had no effect on the highly rigorous efforts he put in as a teacher. He would take the time to explain things to a student. He'd go over and above, staying after school, searching for extra resources, whatever it took. He'd pay attention to implicit signals, like if someone was struggling with schoolwork or even non-schoolwork -- and he'd follow through and offer his guidance/support to them.

      Mr. S did a lot for me personally. He coached me when I came to him with one of my female autist problems. He answered all my questions (even the ones about weed, haha). He read my college application essays. He practiced the interviews with me. He would sit in lunch to talk with me about life. Jeez. What a great man. I mean, who dafuqqqq does all that? Actually, I have to say I was lucky in high school. Most of my teachers were like that -- it's just that he happens to be my favorite and he did the most for me.

      Mr. S was not a lazy man. He was adventurous and well-traveled. He took care of his health: He ate healthy, stayed fit, and spent a lot of time outdoors. He was intelligent and curious, always asking questions and sharing his knowledge. He rarely got angry (this is impressive for a high school teacher). He responded to all situations with patient calmness or humor; his emotional stability was high. And he was really such a kind, caring soul. I try to be everything Mr. S is.

      I saw Mr. S's life as the kind I wanted for myself as well. He is happily married to Mrs. S (my history teacher, also a big influence on me), and they're living their dream. They have two kids together; they've already lived and taught abroad; they make time for their family, their friends, hobbies and learning new things; they have a noble career, where they can inspire youth. They're living a simple but sweet and satisfying life -- I see it as perfect.

      Not only am I personally inspired by him, but I view him as the standard for what I want in a man as well. If I ever find a man as good as he, I will make him my husband. It'd be hard for me to summarize all the things he taught me. I was so lucky to spend three years being influenced by him.
Today is my most influential mentor's birthday; I'll commemorate him here. He taught me about magnanimity, relationships, intellectual discourse, and happiness. He's the best man I've ever known!
